summary:
In southern Africa, one satellite recorded about five times as many fire detections as another over the same region and years. Joining their records directly can make a change of sensor look like a surge in fire activity.

Fire Atlas makes 26 years of satellite fire detections comparable on a common scale. Using overlapping observations from NASA FIRMS, we trained a two-stage LightGBM model to estimate historical detection counts on the S-NPP VIIRS scale from MODIS measurements. In global validation, the model reduced mean absolute log error by about 14% compared with a ratio-based baseline.

On the interactive map, users can draw an area, compare a selected month with the same month in earlier years, check the data source, and export the results. In a study area near Chongqing, August 2022 had about 420 VIIRS-equivalent detections, nearly seven times the historical August median. Fire Atlas helps researchers and land managers distinguish seasonal patterns from unusual months and decide where to investigate further.
details:
Fire Atlas: One Fire Record Across Two Satellite Generations

https://github.com/team-inspiratio/inspiratio-space-apps-2026-challenge

What we built

Fire Atlas is an interactive atlas for exploring monthly satellite fire detections from November 2000 through October 2026. Users can draw a rectangle on a global map or enter coordinates, select a month, compare it with earlier years, and export the monthly series or calendar image. The atlas uses a harmonized record that puts detections from two generations of satellite instruments on a common scale.

Consider a rectangle near Chongqing, China, bounded by 106°–108° E and 29°–30.5° N. Select August 2022 and the atlas shows approximately 420 VIIRS-equivalent detections. Across 21 eligible earlier Augusts, the median was 62, so the selected month was about 6.8 times the historical median and higher than every August in that reference set. The source is labeled Scaled NOAA‑20, telling the user that the value came from NOAA‑20 observations converted to the reference sensor’s scale. The rectangle is a study area, and the result describes satellite detections across that area.

This example shows what we wanted the atlas to make possible. A user can start with a place and a month, see whether it stands out for that season, and check how the underlying value was produced before using it in further analysis.

Why the satellite records needed harmonization

NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) distributes active-fire detections from both MODIS and VIIRS. MODIS has a longer record, while the 375 m VIIRS active-fire product can detect smaller hotspots than the 1 km MODIS product. In southern Africa, during 2014–2021, S‑NPP VIIRS recorded approximately 4.8–5.6 times as many annual detections as Aqua MODIS over the same region and years. Joining the two records directly can make the instrument change look like a sudden increase in fire activity.

Our approach was to learn a conversion from years when the instruments overlapped. For each location and month, we used MODIS measurements to estimate how many detections S‑NPP VIIRS would have recorded. This provides a reference scale for comparing historical months while retaining directly observed VIIRS counts where the release’s observation rules allow.

How we prepared the data

We used four active-fire products from NASA FIRMS. Terra MODIS and Aqua MODIS supplied the model inputs. S‑NPP VIIRS supplied the reference observations and training labels. NOAA‑20 VIIRS provided an observation-based continuation for eligible months with incomplete S‑NPP coverage, after conversion to the S‑NPP scale.

The data pipeline processed approximately 529 million source records, retaining approximately 444 million after quality control. We used annual archives and the FIRMS API, with a sample cross-check between the two delivery routes. We removed duplicate detections, applied sensor-specific confidence filters, and used fire-type information or a static heat-source mask to screen records as appropriate. We kept counts and samples of the records removed at each step so the cleaning decisions could be reviewed.

We then aggregated detections by 0.25° latitude–longitude cell and UTC calendar month. This gave us a common unit for pairing sensors, training the model, and building the monthly calendar. We used the FIRMS missing-data record to track observation completeness. A month with valid coverage and zero detections remains distinguishable from a month with an observation gap. That distinction matters both for model evaluation and for the atlas’s historical comparisons.

How we trained and selected the model

We paired MODIS features with S‑NPP VIIRS counts for the same grid cell and month. The regional model used overlapping observations from January 2014 through June 2021 in California, Córdoba, and southern Africa. Features included Terra and Aqua detection counts, summaries of fire radiative power, nighttime detection share, the number of days with detections, neighboring-cell activity, latitude, and calendar month. Calendar month captures seasonal context. Year, region name, and VIIRS measurements were excluded from the predictor inputs so the conversion could be applied to earlier years with MODIS data alone.

We compared four methods:

  • Direct splice (M0). Use the original sensor counts across the transition. This quantified the discontinuity we wanted to address.
  • Shrinkage ratio (M1s). Learn a MODIS-to-VIIRS multiplier from overlapping observations and pull estimates based on sparse local data toward a more stable pooled ratio. This tested how much a simpler conversion could achieve.
  • Quantile mapping (QM). Match a MODIS count’s position in its historical distribution to the corresponding position in the VIIRS distribution. This tested whether aligning the distributions would also improve estimates for individual months.
  • Two-stage LightGBM (E028). First estimate the probability of any VIIRS detection in a cell-month. Then use a regression model trained on positive cell-months to estimate the count. The regression uses a Tweedie objective, and the prediction is set to zero when the first-stage probability falls below the selected threshold. This lets the model learn the occurrence of detections and their magnitude separately.

We used later years to fit models and earlier years to validate them, mirroring the direction in which the model would be used to reconstruct the historical record. We logged 37 experiments, reviewed the leading candidates for leakage, and selected E028 under predefined scoring and selection rules. The final configuration was frozen before the blind test. The model worked at the cell-month level, while evaluation also aggregated cells into sampled rectangles and scored their monthly totals. This tested the scale at which a person actually uses the atlas when drawing a region.

What the validation showed

We separated two questions in the regional blind test. Could the model reconstruct earlier years in familiar regions? Could it transfer to regions whose VIIRS observations were held out during development? A GitHub Actions workflow scored the sealed predictions against the withheld observations in a single blind run.

Our main metric was mean absolute log error (MALE), which measures the difference between log(estimated count + 1) and log(observed count + 1). Lower is better. We evaluated zero and low detection counts separately because a model can improve aggregate error while performing worse in quiet months.

  • Regional blind test — earlier years in training regions. E028 achieved a MALE of 0.258, compared with 0.332 for the shrinkage-ratio baseline, a 22% reduction.
  • Regional blind test — geographically held-out regions. E028 achieved a MALE of 0.644, compared with 0.857 for the shrinkage-ratio baseline, a 25% reduction.
  • Global validation — the refitted model used in V2. Across two validation windows, the global refit achieved a MALE of 0.534, compared with 0.619 for the shrinkage-ratio baseline, about a 14% reduction.

The regional test showed a clear trade-off. E028 improved the main metric in held-out regions, while its error there was about 2.5 times its error in the earlier-year test in familiar regions. In held-out cases where VIIRS recorded zero detections, E028 estimated at least one detection 11.9% of the time, compared with 2.9% for the shrinkage ratio. That result matters when interpreting small estimated totals in unfamiliar areas.

We also tested the atlas’s historical comparison directly. We used both modeled and observed counts to classify months as high, normal, or low relative to historical values for the same calendar month. Agreement, measured by Cohen’s kappa, was 0.686 in the earlier-year blind test and 0.534 in the geographically held-out test. As a separate plausibility check, we compared the fire detection record with GFED4.1s burned area. In southern Africa, the harmonized record averaged about 2.77 detections per square kilometer of burned area before the transition, compared with 2.92 for the later VIIRS observations. Directly splicing Aqua MODIS to VIIRS would have changed that ratio from about 0.55 to 2.92. GFED was used as a comparison dataset for this check.

The global model powering V2 was refitted on eligible global grid cells using the selected E028 configuration and boosting rounds. It outperformed the shrinkage ratio in 10 of 14 GFED regions across the two validation windows. The one-time blind test scores belong to the regional model. We report the global refit’s results from its separate validation windows.

How we turned the model into a usable global atlas

The global release contains 278,192 grid cells across 312 months, or approximately 86.8 million cell-months. A single sequence can contain direct S‑NPP observations, scaled NOAA‑20 observations, MODIS-based estimates, and lower-confidence estimates that use a Terra-to-Aqua bridge. The app carries those source labels into the calendar and exports so users can see how a value was obtained. Where published regional stability ranges are available, they describe how much model estimates moved when we retrained on resampled years. The regional blind tests showed weaker coverage in unfamiliar regions, so these ranges have limited ability to capture geographic bias.

To make the global release usable in a browser, we published compressed geographic partitions and a catalog of their coverage. When a user draws a rectangle, V2 loads the partitions that intersect it. Boundary cells contribute in proportion to their area of overlap with the rectangle. Demonstration regions that duplicate cells in the global partitions are excluded from custom-area totals, and the app checks for duplicate cells and inconsistent time axes before returning a result. The selection logic also handles rectangles crossing the international date line.

The atlas compares a selected month with earlier, complete records from the same calendar month. It reports a historical median and percentile and assigns a high, normal, or low classification when at least 10 eligible reference years are available. This keeps seasonal changes meaningful. For example, the Chongqing case compares one August with earlier Augusts. Maps, calendars, tables, and exports share the selected area and date range.

We used Python for processing and validation, LightGBM for the harmonization model, Parquet for the analytical dataset, and JavaScript, Leaflet, and Vite for the web application. The build process verifies the published data assets against SHA‑256 checksums so the browser application can be traced back to a specific data release.

Intended impact and limitations

The atlas is designed for researchers and fire or land-management planners who want to compare seasonal patterns, find months worth investigating, and export a documented series for use alongside weather, burned-area, or ground observations. Its contribution is to make a cross-sensor record explorable at the scale a user selects, with the source and quality of each month visible alongside the result.

The values represent satellite fire detections on the S‑NPP VIIRS scale. A single fire can produce multiple detections, and detection coverage varies with observation conditions. Early Terra-only estimates, scaled NOAA‑20 months, low-activity areas, and estimates for unfamiliar regions warrant particular care. A high historical percentile identifies a month worth investigating. Establishing the cause, perimeter, or severity of an individual event requires additional evidence.
